So when we say normal, I think this is important for everybody watching or listening. Normal in medicine means common, not non-pathological. Okay. Not bad, you know, doesn't mean it's not bad. And so norms shifting, meaning we're getting sicker as a population and we're willing to accept lower levels, although they're not optimal for health. The lab reference range, what they say when you get your blood work drawn and you see the reference range, is based on population averages. And so if the population is more anemic, this is going to accept lower levels being normal, even though they're by no means optimal. And I think that's one thing we all talk about is, well, how are you feeling? Your symptomology, what do we see? And it could be the reason why. False assurance. Yeah, exactly. Okay. So despite a lot of controversial things that might have been said in the rest of the episode, I actually mostly agree with the core claims being made here with a few caveats that I'll explain. So as mentioned, ferritin is the body's primary iron storage protein. It's also the preferred lab test for assessing iron status. Much more accurate than measuring iron levels in the blood and a lot less painful and invasive than the gold standard test of doing a bone marrow biopsy to measure a person's iron stores. There are some caveats and nuances to interpreting ferritin levels in practice, especially among patients with inflammatory conditions, those with liver disease, kidney disease, but we'll set those aside for now. The bottom line is if your ferritin is low, you're probably iron deficient. The question though is what is low? So this turns out to not be so simple in practice. Ideally, we can find the sweet spot of where we set this cutoff that gives us the best diagnostic accuracy while minimizing the risk of both false positives and false negatives. Lab tests should, as mentioned in the podcast, also always be interpreted in the context of the person's clinical presentation in order to guide our management strategy. So even if you do have a low ferritin with some iron deficiency, it is often not just as simple as just take some more iron. Now the core issue addressed in this podcast, and one that I actually fully agree with, is that many labs use a lower limit of normal for ferritin that is far too low. You'll often see this cutoff at 12 nanograms per milliliter, 15 nanograms per milliliter, or micrograms per liter. Now why is this? Many lab ranges are set by looking at the distribution of values seen among an apparently healthy population, meaning those without active ongoing signs or symptoms of disease, and arbitrarily setting the cutoff at the lowest 2.5% of values. The problem though is when we examine these same populations and we do that bone marrow biopsy test, we find that 30%, 40%, upwards of 50% of apparently healthy young women, the same types who would be included in these samples, have completely depleted iron stores in their bone marrow. No iron stores. This is most often due to a combination of menstrual blood losses and insufficient dietary intake to keep up with those menstrual blood losses. So if you set a normal cutoff based on descriptive statistics, rather than based on physiology, you're essentially normalizing deficiency. There's actually no physiologic reason why the normal range for ferritin should be fundamentally different between men and women. And so we need to understand iron status on a spectrum. Most people are familiar with the concept of iron deficiency anemia. This is most well recognized, but it also represents the end stage of iron deficiency. When your iron stores are so depleted and have been for so long that it's affected your ability to make red blood cells leading to a low hemoglobin level. But non-anemic iron deficiency is where you have low iron stores, but your hemoglobin might technically still be normal. Our body is quite good at stripping iron out of other tissues like our muscles to prioritize it for blood production. This state is often missed or it's disregarded. And this unfortunately leads to undertreatment. We start to see the consequences of iron deficiency well before people become anemic, if we know what to look for. This suggests that the lower limit of normal is probably higher than most standard lab reference ranges suggest. For example, low iron stores can impair exercise performance and can contribute to symptoms like fatigue. We have multiple double-blind, randomized, controlled trials that have shown that women who are non-anemic but have ferritin levels below 50 can experience significant improvements in their fatigue, their VO2 max, and even their exercise performance when they take supplemental iron. Iron deficiency is also strongly linked to restless leg syndrome as a result of low iron stores in the brain. Supplementation can help, with some evidence suggesting an even higher threshold of at least 75 for this condition. And finally, studies using advanced biomarkers find that the body's methods to compensate for iron depletion don't actually return to their baseline non-deficient levels until ferritin gets at least to 50 or higher. Now, my only point of disagreement with the podcast is the framing that we are progressively more accepting of lower levels, quote, as the population gets sicker. They seem to imply that we are setting new cutoffs based on an increasingly sick, increasingly anemic population, allowing these levels to drift further and further downward, which is just not accurate. While it is true that many reference ranges are set on a sort of convenient sample of an, quote, apparently healthy population, the actual lower limit cutoffs of ferritin have been getting increased in recent years, not decreased due to a sicker population. While the WHO still maintains a general cutoff of just 15 for apparently healthy individuals, in 2020, the American Gastroenterological Association increased their cutoff to 45. The American Society of Hematology currently uses a cutoff of 30 and suggests that you can use 50 for people with signs of iron deficiency or ongoing risk factors like ongoing menstrual blood losses. So while this area is still evolving, these limits are not dropping lower due to a sicker population. As we recognize this, we're actually increasing them as we learn more about the physiology. And so while one side might frame issues with these lab cutoffs as accepting of a more sick population, the other and unfortunately more conspiratorial side tends to frame these things as we're just changing cutoffs so we can sell more drugs. We saw this with changes to recommended blood pressure cutoffs, and blood cholesterol cutoffs. Now it wasn't true in these situations either, but that's a discussion for another day. Sometimes you just can't win. The takeaways here are pretty straightforward. Don't accept a lower limit of say 18 as normal, especially if the person is experiencing symptoms that could be suggestive of iron deficiency, whether or not they have anemia. For most people, using a ferritin lower limit of 50 is reasonable. You could do a lot worse than the recommendation from the podcast of aiming for 60 to 100. I, in my practice, typically use oral or IV iron, intravenous iron, and treat to a target of at least 50 in general and over 75 for those with restless leg syndrome, while also evaluating and treating for the potential causes of iron deficiency, like blood loss or intestinal diseases, absorption problems, et cetera. Ultimately, I do think that we should be testing patients and women in particular more broadly for iron deficiency. We should interpret results based on symptoms and physiology and treat iron deficiency earlier and much more aggressively. So thanks for tuning in, and I look forward to your thoughts and any further discussion on this topic. And that brings us to the end of our review for part one. Now, our goal with this episode wasn't to be negative, but more to provide a filter. There's so much information coming at you from influencers and even credentialed experts on large platforms. So it's vital to distinguish between a mechanism like a hormone spike in isolation and an outcome that actually matters to your life and training, like the amount of strength and endurance gained from exercise or your bone mineral density or having a fall. Now, if you want to train for health, find something that you can do consistently. If you want to get strong, lift weights. And if you're feeling fatigued, we shouldn't overlook anemia. We should still train and auto-regulate it, but don't let the fear of, quote, cortisol or hormone matching keep you from moving your body. But I wanted to actually discuss this a little bit more because I think, and some of this is probably our fault when we talk about the complex relationships of whole foods and how that differs from the isolated nutrients from those foods. We just kind of hand wave it away and say, well, it's the food matrix effect. And people are like, the food, what is Keanu Reeves, the lead star in this particular movie? All right. So let's talk about what the food matrix is and what the food matrix effect is and go from there. The food matrix refers to not only the chemical and physical components of food, but also their molecular relationships that affect how food is digested and metabolized. The food matrix effect refers to how the whole food, like an apple, for example, influences a particular outcome, like feelings of fullness or satiety, or a health parameter compared to one of its nutrients in isolation. So like a particular flavonoid that an apple contains. And so how this might be practically applied is if the study comes out or a mainstream media headline, because I said eating an apple a day keeps the doctor away. Okay. Maybe that came out like turn of the century or whatever. Somebody might say, well, it's the flavonoids or it's the tocopherols or whatever it is, you know? And so they try to isolate and they're successfully able to isolate this thing. And now it's a supplement. You can take, you know, apple flavonoid three, whatever, you know, and they're like, see, I'm taking, I basically, it's like eating apples, but those things are different. Those things are different because the sum of all of the things that makes an apple and apple is greater than the parts. So it's not just the flavonoids, not just, uh, you know, the fiber, for example, or in this case, the protein, but it is the complex relationship of the whole food. And so using the fiber example here, increasing the intake of fiber from whole foods, for example, that tends to be more filling. And so the model that we've been using for exercise technique is called the rep model. It's an acronym. It stands for repeatable, efficient, and that the exercise or the style that you're using, it meets the points of performance. So repeatable means that the individual should perform the exercise in a way where the range of motion, the joint angles, the movement velocity, the tempo, and the overall movement pattern is there's somewhat similar rep to rep. Now, of course, individuals move differently from one another and when the analysis is constrained to a single person from rep to rep. Thus, we're going to accept some rep to rep variability, though the range of motion, the joint angles, the velocity and the tempo should remain fairly similar. That means that your squats should mostly look like squats throughout the set and not squat, squat, squat, good morning, for example. The movement should also be efficient in that it should maximize performance for a given level of energy and effort. In other words, an individual should aim for a technique that minimizes muscular force production that does not contribute to completion of the task. So in a deadlift, for example, if the bar starts way out in front of you and you have to expend all this energy to roll it back, get it into position, and then lift it, that's not very efficient. You can see this when people's hips move up or down prior to the bar leaving the floor, for example. And then finally, the P of the rep model that the movement style meets the points of performance. So these are like pre-specified constraints, like are we going to squat below parallel? Are we going to pause at the bottom? Are we going to use a specific tempo? Is it going to be very fast? So let's talk about some background information here. In conditioning, intensity refers to the metabolic demand of the activity. Now, whether expressed in absolute or relative terms, intensity determines the nature of the physiological stress and individual experiences during exercise, which influences the type of fitness and health adaptations obtained from exercise. For these reasons, exercise prescription should consider intensity based on the expected physiological stress and metabolic demand of the activity for the individual. Now, the current exercise guidelines recommend that all adults complete some combination of at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate intensity or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous intensity conditioning each week, where moderate intensity conditioning exercise correlates to 3.0 to 5.9 metabolic equivalents and vigorous intensity activities are greater than six metabolic equivalents. For completeness, the latest adult compendium of physical activity classifies sedentary activities as 1.0 to 1.5 metabolic equivalents, which just for those listening at home, that means there's a gap. What happens between 1.6 and 2.9 metabolic equivalents? What is that? Just a no man's land? No one knows. Right. Is that just light intensity, I guess so, based on the current compendium? So, in a research setting where oxygen consumption can be directly measured, yeah, METs are probably a suitable instrument for characterizing intensity of an activity. They can also be used in conjunction with exercise duration to calculate total conditioning exercise load in metabolic minutes, MET minutes, with the current guidelines targeting a minimum of 500 to 1,000 MET minutes per week for public health. Outside of these settings, however, I don't think either of us would be on board with using MET-based prescriptions. They're often unpredictable between individuals due to differences in fitness levels, age, medical concerns, training experience, economy movement genetics, and more. So, for example, cycling at 10 miles an hour does not result in the same physiological stress in a young elite cyclist compared to an untrained older individual. And that's very intuitive, although there is a study that actually measured that. You can read about that in the show notes below. I linked it there. Lastly, metabolic equivalents are not easy to understand or monitor by patients or physicians. So, there are a number of other parameters that correlate with exercise intensity, like heart rate, blood lactate levels, oxygen consumption rate, and respiration rate, breathing rate, to name a few. And so, we can think about the intensity of conditioning exercise to be this continuum, ranging from rest to maximal with light, moderate, and vigorous intensity exercise in between. There are a number of thresholds on this continuum that may be useful for exercise prescription. So, the first threshold that I want to discuss is the transition between non-exercise physical activity and exercise. Physical activity is defined as any bodily movement produced by the musculoskeletal system that results in energy expenditure above the basal metabolic rate, whereas exercise in contrast is a subcategory of physical activity that is planned, goal directed towards improving physical fitness. Most activities of daily life would count as physical activity, not exercise. It has been suggested that exercise activities start at about 50% of someone's VO2 max or 60% of their maximum heart rate. For the five zone model of conditioning, right, where zone two has kind of gotten all this hype, this would be the start of zone one. So, below this exercise intensity would just be like regular physical activity activities daily life, but it wouldn't count as exercise. Now, the next threshold is the aerobic threshold. And when determined by blood lactate levels, this is sometimes called lactate threshold number one, which occurs at exercise intensity where blood lactate levels rise to about two millimoles per liter. Lactate levels are otherwise stable because the body is producing and processing it or clearing it at a steady state. Now, when measured by respiratory rates, so how fast someone's breathing, this is called the first ventilatory threshold, since breathing rate has increased compared to resting values. Typical heart rates at this point range between like 65 to 80% of maximal heart rate, although this can vary significantly between individuals. And zone two in the five zone model is right before this threshold. That's important. Remember that. So, right before the aerobic threshold, that's the top of zone two. Once you pass the aerobic threshold, it's probably more zone three in that five zone model. The final threshold that I want to talk about on this continuum going from rest to maximal intensity conditioning exercise is the anaerobic threshold, which occurs at an exercise intensity where blood lactate levels rise even higher as the body is unable to process it quickly enough for removal to keep it at a steady state. Again, when measured by blood lactate levels, this point is also often called lactate threshold number two, and lactate levels are often four millimoles per liter or higher. This point is also called the second ventilatory threshold when measured by the respiratory exchange ratio, which measures the amount of carbon dioxide produced compared to oxygen consumed. Typical heart rates here at this threshold are about 85 to 95% of maximal heart rate, which again varies significantly between individuals. Exercise performed below this anaerobic threshold, but above aerobic threshold, that represents vigorous intensity exercise, whereas exercise above this anaerobic threshold will be considered maximal intensity. So, for your five zone model people, zones three and zone four are below the anaerobic threshold, but above the aerobic threshold, and zone five is above the anaerobic threshold. Modern intensity exercise is below the aerobic threshold, but above the threshold when exercise begins, this is zones one and two in the five zone model. Vigorous intensity exercise is above the aerobic threshold, but below the anaerobic threshold, again this is zones three and four in the five zone model, and then maximal intensity exercise is above the anaerobic threshold. All right, well, let's talk about a little bit of the bro science that ultimately doomed our shit here. One study that gets a lot of airtime, it's been cited a bunch, is this PILS study from 2011. I've seen it actually cited a few times online in the Biohacker and sort of natural testosterone optimization circles. It suggested a link between vitamin D supplementation and testosterone. Now, in the study, a group taking about 3,300 IUs of vitamin D per day for a year increased their testosterone levels from an average of 300 nanograms per deciliter to 380 nanograms per deciliter, whereas those taking a placebo didn't see any changes. So you look at that and you're like, hmm, that's a bump. I want a bump. More testosterone, more gains. There are a few problems with this study. So one, it was not actually designed to test testosterone levels. It was actually a secondary post hoc analysis of a weight loss study. The researchers didn't recruit men to see if vitamin D built muscle or increased testosterone. They just looked back at a small group of 54 dudes who happen to have their testosterone levels measured. Now, in the world of science, when you dig through enough data after a study is already over, you can typically find a correlation with something by sheer coincidence if you look at enough variables. No shade intended, but this is a classic case of data mining being presented as a primary discovery. This happens all the time, unfortunately. The second problem with the study, again, we're talking about 54 people. In a study that small, one or two outliers can completely skew the average. The difference was modest, 300 to 380 nanograms per deciliter, so not crazy. So tiny sample size, the statistical signal can be incredibly noisy there. This is why larger, better-controlled trials and meta-analyses with hundreds of thousands of patients can be better at showing the real relationship. The other problem here is that they used an immunoassay to measure testosterone levels, which is an older type of test that is notoriously unreliable, especially at lower testosterone levels, compared to the new tests we use, which are LC-MS. And then finally, even if we take the study at face value, the increase they found is almost certainly not clinically significant. This slight bump in numbers, which are, they're well within the test's error bars, and the study did not measure, like, muscle protein synthesis. It didn't measure one rep max strength or muscular hypertrophy, body composition, or even symptoms of testosterone deficiency. So, like, a slightly higher number on a lab report, to me, doesn't matter if it doesn't actually change the person's life. We see this all the time. People will take this tiny shift in a surrogate marker, and then, especially with a supplement, and they'll just run with it, market it to the hills. Now, three recent meta-analyses essentially closed the door on this. They looked at the totality of the evidence and found that vitamin D is pretty much a total wash for testosterone levels, regardless if someone has low or normal testosterone levels or low or normal vitamin D levels. So, the analogy I think about here is, like, if you take vitamin D to boost testosterone, it's kind of like trying to fix a car that won't start by adding more gas to the tank. If the engine is the problem, it doesn't matter if your gas tank was bone dry or already half full. Adding more fuel is not going to make the car run. You can keep pumping more and more gas. That's the vitamin D, but you're not fixing the motor. That's the source of the testosterone deficiency. You're just creating potentially a massive spill that could become a fire hazard, or in our patient's case, metastatic calcium deposition. I think that there are reasonable basic principles that should be kind of respected when it comes to selecting a reasonable screening test. And we've talked about these on prior podcasts a bunch. Ideally, it should be a prevalent health problem. It should be something that actually has a accurate and reliable and cost effective test for it. And it should be something that has an asymptomatic latent phase, meaning a period of time when there are no symptoms that would lead to diagnostic testing, during which period you could catch it. And there should be a treatment available that when offered earlier compared with later substantially improves the trajectory of that disease or the person's morbidity and mortality. If all of those criteria are met, you can make a reasonable case for screening for a lot of things. Now, there are many medical conditions out there that will fail one or more of these things. It might be an ultra ultra rare disease that it's not worth screening the whole population for. It might be a condition that actually doesn't have a long asymptomatic latent phase, but rather it will manifest abruptly all of a sudden. It basically showed the limitations of these multi-cancer early detection tests. In a group of over 6,600 people, the test signaled cancer in 92 individuals, but only 35 of those were actually confirmed to have cancer. Now, that gives us a positive predictive value of only 38%. Now, the specificity of the test is marketed as an incredible 99.6%. And a high specificity test means that if you don't have cancer, the test is almost certainly going to return a negative result. But if you do have cancer, it should be positive. It's basically designed to minimize false alarms in healthy people. However, the clinical utility is limited by the sensitivity, which is the test's ability to actually find the cancer when it's present. At stage one, the sensitivity is only 16.8%. That means that for every 100 people with early stage cancer, the test misses 83 of them. Now, by the time you reach stage four, the sensitivity jumps to over 90%, which creates a fundamental paradox in screening. The test is most accurate when the cancer is already advanced and treatment options are limited, but it's least effective at stage one, where medical intervention could theoretically have the highest impact. And then we also have to address the false positive burden. The first model is the substance model, where addictive substances are rarely single agents, just as cigarettes are a complex mixture engineered to deliver nicotine as fast as possible. Well, highly processed foods are complex mixtures of refined carbohydrates and fats designed for rapid absorption. Here, the food is the drug. And then there's the second model. This is the behavioral model. In the food world, well, we haven't found that nicotine. People don't abuse pure sugar or butter outside of like some weird social media trends. So for example, after food restriction and weight loss, humans and rodents' behavior usually changes to a markedly increased intake in calories. And this isn't because the food has changed. === FILE: How to Fix a Training Plateau： A Step-By-Step Guide For Breaking Through [EHUwQzLtU5w].txt ===

 them. For background information, you need to be familiar with the fitness fatigue model, which is used to describe how people adapt and respond to exercise. In this model, performing exercise drives a simultaneous increase in both fitness and fatigue levels. Now, there are many exercise variables that can be adjusted to try to generate more fitness and less fatigue, but there are no free lunches here. More exercise will tend to drive more fitness and more fatigue, whereas less exercise will tend to drive less fitness and less fatigue. All right, with that in mind, let's imagine a lifter who squats 310 pounds for three sets of six reps at an RPE 8. So two reps left in the tank, and he does that on week one. He comes back on week two, and he squats 315 pounds for three sets of six reps, but this time it was a soul-crushing bone-on-bone RPE 10 for each set. It was maximal. No reps left in the tank. First question is, which day was he stronger? You got your answer yet? Now, most people will look at the number on the bar and say that he was stronger on week two. 315 pounds is more than 310 pounds, right? So he's stronger when he squatted more weight. But the fact that the effort was much harder on week two should influence your interpretation. On week one, he did the work each set with two reps left in the tank, meaning he could have definitely squatted 315 pounds if he wanted to. Sure, it might have been a little harder, but it's unlikely that adding a measly five pounds would have made it a 10 out of 10 maximal effort like he experienced on week two. If we compare the two efforts, his performance was either roughly the same or lower on week two as it was compared to week one. If he had actually gotten stronger, he should have been able to lift more weight with the same relative effort, meaning that he should have been able to squat 315 pounds for three sets of six all at RPE 8 or with two reps left in the tank. But since he didn't actually get stronger in the time between the workouts, perhaps maybe even getting weaker, some folks might interpret this as a stall or a training plateau. But why? Was it a lack of fitness adaptations, in this case strength, coming online? Or was it too much fatigue to where the lifter couldn't recover before the next session? Now, if we think it's a lack of fitness, we would need to increase the signal from the exercise program to drive more strength development. We might need more volume, more intensity, or more something to get the wheels turning. In the short term, this is unlikely to immediately produce results as the added training will also drive additional fatigue and the body is going to need some more time to adapt or accommodate to it. If we think it's a lack of recovery, adding more work is like trying to put out a fire with gasoline. In that case, we would need to pull back and reduce the signal from the exercise program. In the short term, this might work to see an increase in strength as reducing the amount of training being done can temporarily increase performance as fatigue is dissipated or bled off. Now, this is how most peaking programs work. But if we reduce the exercise over the long term, we're going to get less of a signal to improve fitness too. Now, in this particular scenario, we don't really know why the lifter didn't get stronger because there's just not enough information. It's only been a week and that just doesn't tell us much. Now, many people react to a one-week stall by panicking. They see the bar speed slow down or the weight stay the same and they immediately want to change their program. They're responding to short-term noise and in doing so, they often destroy the long-term signal. === FILE: How-To Exercise After A Hysterectomy (OB⧸GYN Doc Answers) [ogf3ZpZgXEc].txt ===

  hysterectomy may be performed at the same time as a hysterectomy for certain reasons. If a woman's ovaries are not removed, there are no long-term hormonal consequences of undergoing a hysterectomy. An important caveat is that the ovaries have blood supply from two main blood vessels. A hysterectomy necessarily involves cutting through one of these blood vessels, the ones that exist between the uterus and the ovaries. This can sometimes lead to a temporary decline in ovarian hormones until normal blood flow is compensated through the primary ovarian blood supply. Most women do not experience persistent or perceivable symptoms when the ovaries are left in place. A small fraction do experience symptoms from these hormone fluctuations, although it tends to be temporary. The most common reasons I perform hysterectomies are for abnormal uterine bleeding, for uterine fibroids, and for pelvic pain. The next important consideration is how the hysterectomy will be performed. So this surgery can be performed through the vagina, where there are no incisions in the abdomen. It can be performed laparoscopically, which is done through three to five small incisions on the abdomen. Or it can be done through a single larger abdominal incision. Think like a c-section incision at the bikini line. There are several factors that are considered between the patient and her surgeon to determine which route is the best route for her. Regardless of the surgical route, though, all women who have undergone a total hysterectomy will have a five to eight centimeter internal incision at the top of the vagina, where the cervix used to sit. And that's closed with a dissolvable suture. Most patients who have undergone a hysterectomy can go home the same day as their surgery if it was uncomplicated. Now to the main focus of the question. What kind of activity restrictions should be observed after hysterectomy and for how long? It's important to note that every woman's pain and recovery experience can vary after a hysterectomy. Those with healing abdominal incisions may experience more discomfort in the two to three weeks following surgery. Regardless of the type of surgery they have, though, women who are given liberal or no activity restrictions do just as well, if not marginally better, than those who are given strict and specific restrictions. Evidence actually supports the approach of listening to your body by scaling and modulating your activity types and effort by your baseline abilities and also the pain and discomfort feedback you're feeling with consideration to whether or not you're requiring strong pain medications. So a great example is advising against taking a maximal effort squat, for example, because you've just taken 10 milligrams of oxycodone. One activity that bears mentioning where this doesn't apply, though, is vaginal penetrative intercourse or really any activity that involves insertion of a product or an object into the vagina. Just like you wouldn't subject yourself to blunt forces against a healing row of stitches anywhere else on your body, it's important to remember that concealed and healing incision at the top of the vagina, also known as the vaginal cuff. And its specified healing time should be respected, no matter how well you may be feeling. It's important to await a vaginal exam with a surgeon six to eight weeks after surgery to ensure proper closure and healing of the cuff before resuming intercourse. Unfortunately, there are no great data that guide the return to resistance training after hysterectomy. My recommendation is informed by the last decade practicing as a surgeon and also my experiences as a powerlifter who trained with RPE. I advise delaying return to moderate to high intensity resistance training until the vaginal cuff is cleared, although lower intensity activities such as walking, recumbent biking, and seated upper body exercises are often acceptable and encouraged in the early period after surgery. This is all in addition to activities of daily living. The post-operative judgment of the surgeon of when a woman can resume intercourse can be used to correspond with a return to progressively heavier training. Hope you found this helpful.

=== FILE: Hypertrophy for Strength Athletes [INHi9m-zWMY].txt ===

All right, related does a strength athlete ever achieve enough hypertrophy? Is there a point in the athletes development whether there is no longer a need to make the muscle larger and only to make them stronger? It's a complicated question. So enough hypertrophy. IMean, that's like saying, you know, you ever get jacked enough. You ever make too much money? IMean, I don't know that you can say yes to that. So as far as in an athletes development where they no longer need to make the muscles larger and only need to make them stronger, that assumes that these happen independently. And I don't know that I view them as like two independent processes. I think that the amount of muscle mass increase that occurs, that co-ocurs with strength increase particularly at high level strength athletes is much smaller than when a occurs in like physique athletes, bodybuilders, et cetera, who are primarily just trening for size increases and not at all for strength increases. But I think that there's still some hypertrophy occurring nonetheless even if it's relatively small. Now that being said, the actual hypertrophy process is rather complicated as far as like does the myophibrular hypertrophy just the contractile protein? Is that precede some of the sarcoplasma hypertrophy which tends to create a more substantial increase in muscle cross-sectional area or does the one, you know, precede the other. That stuff's still being assessed out. And so this is still an active area of research. But for from a practical standpoint, I think trying to get as jacked as possible using what while still doing the specific exercises, the specific for your sport and the correct intensity ranges to make them go up would be the goal. I don't ever think you say, I'm jacked enough. I'm going to cut the volume down. Yeah, this part last part of this question or it says there's no longer a need to make the muscles larger and only to make them stronger. I think that creates an kind of an artificial dichotomy or separation between those two things. When really, at least there's there is to be fair some debate in the research world about how much hypertrophy contributes to strength development and performance. But I tend to lean on the side and I think you probably do too that strength performance of a particular muscle, one of the contributing factors to that strength potential is muscle size. The other major contributor would be the neurological like the skill, the recruitment kind of aspect of it. And so you can't really say I don't need to make the muscle larger and only to make it stronger when muscle size is probably a contributor to muscle strength. And so I think that to the extent that you want to continue making your muscle stronger, you should strive to make them larger as well. And I don't think there's actually a way for you to aim to make them stronger without generating some amount of hypertrophy along the way in the process.

It's one of many different types of irregular heart rhythms, and it happens when the atria, or what are commonly known as the top chambers of the heart, essentially start fibrillating. And that's a fancy word to say. They're just essentially quivering. They're not contracting in a kind of metronomic, regular, effective fashion. So they are electrically very irritable. They're just quivering, not really contributing much to blood flow from the top chambers into the bottom chambers. There can be a lot of other associated symptoms with this. General fatigue, exercise intolerance, things like that can happen. But also as blood kind of sits in those top chambers and doesn't really flow as effectively as it otherwise should, anytime blood sits still, it's going to want to clot. And it can clot. And then if you have a clot sitting in your heart, that can get shot out of your heart to lots of different potential places in your body. If it gets shot up to your brain, it can give you a stroke. If it gets shot down to your leg, you can get acute leg, you know, limb ischemia. It can get shot into your spleen or your kidneys, lots of other different potential places. So these patients are often either, you know, shocked out of atrial fibrillation into a regular heart rhythm, put on medicines to get them out of atrial fibrillation into a regular heart rhythm. Sometimes we let people live in atrial fibrillation if it's been, you know, longstanding for a really long period of time and we're not going to be able to effectively get them out of it. And then most of these patients are going to get put on some form of blood thinner to reduce that risk of clotting because that can lead to potentially catastrophic consequences. Yeah. Yeah. And the reality is that hormonal contraception does not substantially impair or enhance sports performance at a population level. The next myth to address here is that bone density will diminish or disappear in women taking birth control pills. And this is a major exaggeration. Estrogen is crucial for bone health as it helps to maintain and build bone. Combined hormonal contraceptives, which contain estrogen, generally have a neutral or even mildly beneficial effect on bone density in adults. For adolescents, the nuance is important. And that is that starting combined hormonal contraceptive soon after menarche or the first period may temporarily slow the speed at which the body builds peak bone mass. But to suggest that healthy women are left with no bone density is fear-mongering, and it is not supported by data. Consistent training, adequate nutrition, and avoiding gonadotoxins like cigarette smoke and certain drug regimens are the biggest drivers of long-term bone health, in fact. And the next topic to address or myth to bust is that combined hormonal contraceptives shut off testosterone. The combination of claims that this came from were, first, there's no way I'm going to let her testosterone levels drop. That was in reference to the adolescent niece. In reference to women who take hormonal contraceptives, presumably to reduce symptoms of hyperandrogenism, such as acne and excessively oily skin, that is a presumption, as that speaker referenced PCOS specifically. And the reality is that these claims are misleading because it confuses total testosterone with bioavailable or free testosterone. So let's talk about what combined hormonal contraceptives actually do. The estrogen in these combined hormonal options increases a protein called sex hormone binding globulin. That's made in our livers. Think of sex hormone binding globulin as a taxi service for hormones. The result is when you have more sex hormone binding globulin taxis, they pick up the free testosterone in your bloodstream. This means that you have less unbound testosterone available to interact with tissues like muscle, bone, and skin. This is why doctors prescribe combined hormonal contraceptives for conditions like severe acne. Since unbound testosterone affects the skin in ways that lead to increased skin oil production and acne. So what is the impact on performance? Well, when women taking combined hormonal contraceptives have less free testosterone, studies actually do not show a clinically significant impact on strength or sports performance. We cannot simplistically apply male performance models to female physiology, specifically that we will run faster or lift more weight linearly with higher levels of bioavailable testosterone. Women are not little men, and our bodies respond differently to changes in androgens. Pivoting away from myth-busting of some of the claims made on this podcast, I'd like to emphasize the importance of focusing on the individual. Beyond the science, we have to consider the lived experience of the athlete in this case. And I would maintain that quality of life is a significant performance factor. In any case, motor neurons, motor neurons, what these are, these are nerves that go from your spinal cord to your muscles, your skeletal muscles. And so specifically what happens as people age is that these alpha motor neurons, these specifically the ones that innervate or connect to your high threshold, fast twitch or type two muscle fibers, these things die. And when these neurons die, a nearby slow neuron tends to sprout a branch to try to go rescue this abandoned muscle fiber. So the muscle fiber itself, if it's connected by one of these sprouts, one of these branches, the muscle fiber typically survives, but then it's converted to a slow twitch or type one muscle fibers. So you lose your high gear from these type two muscle fibers, which is why you lose power first. You lose this writing reflex, the ability to catch yourself when you trip or rising quickly from a chair. And so that's why people fall and ultimately can fracture a hip, for example. This selective loss of type two muscle fibers explains why muscle power declines so much faster than strength, and why strength declines so much faster than muscle size, and that's why falls are common with aging. This kind of leads into this reversibility sort of question, like, can we reverse sarcopenia? Well, you can't regrow a dead motor neuron, you can only strengthen the ones that are left, and this is why prevention tends to be superior to treatment. And so we've got tons of evidence on this. If you take a muscle biopsy of an individual sarcopenia and you look at it under a microscope, you see a dramatic shrinking of the type two muscle fibers by up to 50%, while type one muscle fiber size tends to be the same. And at age 70, an individual may lose 25 to 50% of their alpha motor neurons compared to what they had when they were age 20. And so the next question then becomes, well, why? Why does this happen? Well, these type two muscle fibers, these fast-twitch muscle fibers, they cost a lot. The metabolic demand of these muscle fibers is higher. They also require a lot of signaling from the environment to maintain them. So mechanotransduction, loading them, being active with them, compared to type one muscle fibers that are just like postural, for example, and you're gonna use them regardless of if you exercise or not. And ultimately with this disuse, not only do the muscle fibers like not have any reason to stick around, but the actual satellite cells or stem cells for the muscles that we call satellite cells basically become unresponsive. And so you lose not only the muscle fiber, right? It changes its morphology and the nerve also kind of goes away, but also the machinery you had to repair the muscle fiber when it gets damaged also goes away. And it's mostly from disuse, although again, we can't completely stop this aging, this biological clock. It doesn't just build muscle, but it changes the survival rate of these type two, these fast-twitch muscle fibers that are typically destined to die. So Dr. Baraki, what is anabolic resistance and why is it so important here? Yeah, it is a concept, another one that we've been talking about for a long time, and we're kind of more formally addressing here, it's this idea that when you deliver at what we'll call a dose of anabolic stimulus to somebody, and those anabolic stimuli tend to be most importantly physical training, or mechanical stimulus to the body, to the muscles, and secondarily to that dose of, say, dietary protein, amino acids, for example, different people will have a different anabolic response to that dose. So some people might mount a very large anabolic response, a lot of muscle protein synthesis, and others might display a more blunted anabolic response, or a lesser degree of muscle protein synthesis. And in this situation that we're calling anabolic resistance, it is kind of the term used to describe that more blunted response to anabolic stimulus. We tend to see it more often in older folks, although again, I kind of hesitate to ascribe it to aging alone, just like when we hesitated to ascribe sarcopenia to aging alone. Anabolic resistance we know is more common in the context of that, what I called multi morbidity, or when people have multiple, you know, concomitant medical conditions, especially in the like very acute settings. So for example, if somebody is admitted to the ICU with a raging illness or bad case of sepsis, multi organ failure or something like that, we know that they tend to be very, very anabolically resistant, not to mention that they're generally laid up in bed nearly 24 hours a day, things like that. But even outside of this condition with complex medical conditions, acute conditions and chronic conditions, those who tend to be less physically active or have more sedentary behavior in general, that tends to be a significant contributor, especially as folks get older as well. Now, we know that this phenomenon of anabolic resistance is not destiny, it is not permanent, it is something that can be overcome if we adjust that dose of stimulus that we deliver to the person. So this has also been studied to where, for example, in exercise contexts, increasing the volume and or the intensity of activity that is being delivered to the person can restore a degree of sensitivity to that anabolic stimulus, meaning that whereas somebody who is generally sedentary and not moving around and then they might do a set or two sets or something of an exercise might get a lesser anabolic response, if we increase that to three sets or four sets or push the intensity a little bit higher of their conditioning activity, we tend to see a more significant muscular response to that activity. And similarly, when we give them a dose of 10 or 15 or 20 grams of dietary protein, including in particular the amino acid leucine, where it might be a gram or two of that, in that dose of protein of up to say 20 grams, they might have a lesser response in terms of their muscle protein synthesis. But if you increase that to 30 grams of protein or even 40 grams of protein, you might restore that anabolic response. I think that this has been taken, maybe because it's telling some people what they want to hear based on their bias of what we'll call it protein maxing these days, to where they think that, oh, if this is, as people get older, they just need to have more and more massive amounts of protein and that'll solve this issue. But this has also been looked at and just increasing protein intake does not meaningfully impact outcomes in these types of situations. It is supportive of adaptation and recovery and things like that to the training, but on its own, you are unlikely to build a significant degree more muscle just by increasing the dietary protein alone. And so for that reason, both of us I think tend to emphasize way more importantly, the idea of the physical activity, the training, as well as addressing any reversible underlying health factors that you can actually address to restore that degree of sensitivity. So electrodiagnostic studies were ordered, which are divided into two parts here, one nerve conduction study, and then electromyography, which you might know better as EMG. Now for the listeners at home, you can think of the nerve conduction studies as a technician testing a fiber optic cable. They tap into one end of the nerve, they send a pulse down it, and they measure three specific things. First, they measure latency. This is the time it takes for the signal to start, essentially the reaction time of the nerve. Second, they measure amplitude. This is the strength or the volume of the signal, which tells us how many individual nerve fibers or axons are actually alive and functioning. And third, they test velocity, the speed at which the signal travels down the wire, which tells us if the insulation or myelin sheath is still intact. Now in this patient, when they tested the motor division of the common peroneal nerve, the results were definitive, non-recordable across the board, no latency, no amplitude, and no measurable velocity. These are the nuts and bolts of a program like the exercises, the reps schemes, the rep ranges, the intensity, rest periods, the tempo of the movement or velocity, range of motion, etc. This can also be conceptualized as the external load. The trening stress is the resultant load placed upon the individual based on their current level of fitness and performance potential and everything that goes into that. Like their mood, their trening expectations, nutrition status, fatigue, etc. This can also be classified as the internal load and can be measured by rate of perceived exertion, changes in heart rate, etc. Fitness adaptations are the positive, physiological, and psychological effects of exercise, like strength, hypertrophy, cardiovascular fitness, improved cognitive performance, etc. Fatigue can be conceptualized as the negative, physiological, and psychological effects of exercise. Things like soreness, muscle damage, reduced force production, tiredness, etc. Performance potential is the ratio or balance of fitness adaptations relative to fatigue at any given point in a specific environment for completing a particular task. Thus, trening stimulus produces a given trening stress that is unique to the individual, which subsequently results in both fitness adaptations and fatigue. The principle of progressive overload suggests that the human body must be continually challenged by greater and greater trening stimuli over time in order to drive fitness adaptations. And so when the body recognizes something as foreign, again, it could be a drug, it could be a pathogen, it could be not a pathogen, but something you're allergic to, it could be even your own body if you have an autoimmune disease, then it produces antibodies and other kind of immune effectors against that thing. And so if a drug or a substance that we're giving somebody itself is immunogenic, then we have concerns that it is going to be ineffective altogether or it might progressively lose its efficacy as the immune system learns to either prevent it from doing its thing or accelerating its clearance by way of antibodies or other immune mediated responses. And this tells the liver to actively dump fat and burn calories for energy, really mostly heat in this case. So it addresses both sides of the calories in versus calories out equation. As far as the human data on this is pretty good. They just wrapped up Triumph 4, this showed an unprecedented 28.7% weight loss at 68 weeks. And this was for individuals with obesity and knee osteoarthritis. So in these individuals, yeah, the average weight loss was 28.7% up to 71 pounds at 68 weeks. And beyond just weight loss, it reduced knee pain as measured by the Womax scale by 76%, demonstrating that the weight loss and potentially other effects of the medication improved pain experience. By comparison, the placebo group only lost 2.1% of their body weight. Also has some interesting effects on metabolic associated sciatic liver disease, also known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. They had a phase two trial on this and it showed a pretty impressive clearance of liver fat that had been accumulated. Over 85% of patients achieved complete resolution of the fat that was in their liver. That's defined as having less than 5% liver fat at 48 weeks, which we think is due to the glucagon receptor agonism that this drug adds. As far as the toxicity and side effect profile, unfortunately, there does seem to be a higher side effect profile, particularly at max doses. There was an 18% dropout rate in this latest trial, and it does seem to increase resting heart rate by about 5 beats per minute, which does require some monitoring. So there are some concerns there, particularly at max doses. To me, retachrotide represents a massive shift in how we approach fat loss. In the past, the only way we knew how to rev the engine was through stimulants like aphedra, which essentially dumped adrenaline to the system to force a higher heart rate and a higher metabolic rate to ultimately burn more calories. Now, retachrotide achieves a similar metabolic increase, but it does so through hormonal signaling, specifically through the glucagon receptor rather than the catecholamine dump. It is a more sophisticated way to turn up the furnace. And that's what makes retachrotide so different from the previous generations of anti-BC medications like ozampic or Zepbound. While older drugs mostly focused on slowing down the gut and telling the brain you're full, retachrotide is actively increasing energy expenditure through thermogenesis. It's essentially turning up the heat in the fat cells and the liver.
